details:
Problem

------------------------

From my perspective, the current networking options in Udon have been designed in an oversimplified manner. I perceive the intention was making to make things easier for beginners, which is nice, but has come at a cost to advanced programmers.

[UdonSynced], Ownership semantics, and SendNetworkEvent; All of them work great for their intended simple usages, but are virtually useless building blocks for building sophisticated networked systems. I understand part of the design constraints is that no world-code will run on the server which leads to the inception of such ideas.

Suggestion

-------------------------

For the existing primitives to work, of course, VRChat sends data from one client to another over some form of socket/connection. As an advanced programmer, all I want is access to the foundation, the communication line between players. It is greatly preferable to just have a primitive which I can write bytes into, and get bytes back out.

The usage in udon# could be as simple as these two non-blocking functions:

// Write bytes to remote player.

Networking.Write( remote_player_id, channel_id, ref buffer, buffer_length );

// Read bytes coming from remote player. 

int length = Networking.Read( remote_player_id, channel_id, ref buffer, buffer_length );

Design thoughts

-----------------------

For a gaming networking API, I think ValveNetworkingSockets has the best paradigm for their sockets:

"Connection-oriented API (like TCP)

... but message-oriented (like UDP), not stream-oriented.

Supports both reliable and unreliable message type"

It would make sense in the simplest implementation to just have a reliable message protocol, but having the option of both would be ideal.

A simple consideration for network traffic is to just have a limit of the number of bytes you can send per second, similar to how the limits are specified for [UdonSynced].

If there is something I'm missing from a security perspective, I would be interested to hear.
title: (udon) Please reconsider networking primitives; Sockets preferred to abstraction.
